# Command reference

[中文](../zh-CN/commands.md)

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-cli-docs.mjs from the command line's own tables — do not edit; after changing a command run node scripts/gen-cli-docs.mjs -->

This page lists every `daisy` command; each block is exactly what `daisy <command> --help` prints.

There are two kinds of commands:

- **Local commands** manage the Daisy process and files on this machine; they work while Daisy is not running.
- **API commands** call the running Daisy through the local API. Everything the web page can do is here, except answering the AI's tool approvals and questions (only on the web page and paired devices).

A few rules hold for all of them:

- Commands marked “needs the PIN” prompt for the PIN in the terminal first.
- Credentials (PIN, API key, authorization code) are read from a prompt or standard input, never from the command line, so they stay out of the shell history.
- API commands print their answer as JSON on standard output; on an error they say what happened and what to do, and exit non-zero.
- The global option `--data-dir <dir>` (or the `DAISY_DATA` environment variable) picks another data directory; `--lang <language>` (or `DAISY_LANG`) another language.

The HTTP API behind the API commands is in the [local API reference](../../api/local-api.md).

## Overview

```text
daisy — the Daisy command line

Usage: daisy <command> [subcommand] [arguments] [options]

Local commands (manage the Daisy process and files on this machine; they work while Daisy is not running):
  start       Start Daisy in the background (if it is already running, just say so)
  stop        Stop Daisy (a running turn ends and is marked interrupted, never replayed)
  status      Whether Daisy is running, where it listens, whether the PIN is set, autostart and updates
  open        Open the local web page (a link with a one-time passcode)
  update      See, check for or switch to a new version (waits for idle, backs up first, rolls back on failure)
  doctor      Self-check: Node version, data directory permissions, whether each harness is installed and signed in, PIN, ports, autostart
  uninstall   Clean up before uninstalling: stop Daisy and remove autostart; the data directory is kept
  autostart   Turn start-at-login on or off (Linux: a systemd user unit; macOS: a launchd login item; Windows: the current user's Run entry; never needs root / administrator)
  watch       Follow the event outlet: AI approval requests, AI questions and calls waiting for approval, as they appear and are settled

API commands (through the local API: everything the web page can do, except answering the AI's tool approvals and questions):
  access      external off, external on, issuer refresh, issuer remove, issuer set, issuer show …
  agent       act set, act show, audience set, audience show, list, public set …
  approval    comment add, comment list, list, show
  attachment  download, upload
  audit       list, logs
  call        list, show
  contact     export, import, inspect, list, remove, show …
  device      list, revoke
  events      list, snapshot
  grant       list, revoke
  language    set, show
  login       cancel, input, list, show, start
  notify      list, set, show
  pair        Make a pairing code (daisy pair): another device that enters it connects as the owner
  pin         reset, set, status
  profile     auto-compact restart, auto-compact show, create, create-managed, delete, update
  prompt      layers apply, layers apply-cancel, layers forget-node, layers set, layers show, mine set …
  relay       off, set, show
  request     decide, list, show
  restart     cancel, request, status
  session     activity, background stop, cancel, create, delete, events …
  token       issue, list, revoke
  whoami      Who am I: the owner, through which channel, on which face
  workspace   add, browse, browse-result, catalog

First use: daisy start → daisy pin set → daisy open (sign in to a harness and create a session on the web page)

Global options:
  --data-dir <dir>    use this data directory (default: the system's convention; or set DAISY_DATA)
  --lang <language>   use this language (en, zh-CN; or set DAISY_LANG; default: the setting, else the system's)
  -h, --help          help; every command has it: daisy <command> --help
  -V, --version       version
```

## Local commands

### daisy start

```text
Usage: daisy start [--port <port>] [--foreground]

Start Daisy in the background (if it is already running, just say so)

With autostart on (daisy autostart on), systemd (Linux) or launchd (macOS) starts it; otherwise it starts as a background process and writes its output to logs/daisy.log in the data directory.
On macOS, turn autostart on first: launchd starts it in your login session, the only way Claude's keychain sign-in can be read.
No port needed: it is derived from the account's uid, and if that one is taken a free one is found and remembered. The data directory follows the system's convention; --data-dir or DAISY_DATA changes it.

Options:
  --port <port>     the local face's port, 1024–65535 (an error if it is taken, never silently changed)
  --foreground      run in the foreground in this terminal (for debugging, or for another service manager)

Common options: --data-dir <dir> (default: the system's convention, or DAISY_DATA); --lang <language> (or DAISY_LANG)
```

### daisy stop

```text
Usage: daisy stop

Stop Daisy (a running turn ends and is marked interrupted, never replayed)

Sends SIGTERM and waits for it to wrap up: a running turn is marked interrupted (principle 2, never replayed), web connections close, then it exits. Under systemd it uses systemctl --user stop; under launchd, launchctl bootout.
Autostart stays as it is: it starts again at the next boot (to turn that off: daisy autostart off).

Common options: --data-dir <dir> (default: the system's convention, or DAISY_DATA); --lang <language> (or DAISY_LANG)
```

### daisy status

```text
Usage: daisy status [--json]

Whether Daisy is running, where it listens, whether the PIN is set, autostart and updates

Exit code: 0 running; 3 not running.

Options:
  --json    print JSON (for scripts and AIs)

Common options: --data-dir <dir> (default: the system's convention, or DAISY_DATA); --lang <language> (or DAISY_LANG)
```

### daisy open

```text
Usage: daisy open [--external] [--print]

Open the local web page (a link with a one-time passcode)

Asks Daisy for a one-time passcode (valid for 10 minutes, works once) and opens the link carrying it in the browser; prints the link when no browser can be opened.

Options:
  --external   a link for another machine (through the outside face: the direct address of the outside face's listener when it is on, with the relay's address listed as an alternative; the relay's fixed address when there is only a relay; first run daisy access external on or daisy relay set). This lets someone in, so it needs the PIN
  --print      only print the link, don't open the browser

Common options: --data-dir <dir> (default: the system's convention, or DAISY_DATA); --lang <language> (or DAISY_LANG)
```

### daisy update

```text
Usage: daisy update [--check | --apply [--from <tgz>] [--allow-downgrade] | --rollback | --source <source> | --now | --cancel]

See, check for or switch to a new version (waits for idle, backs up first, rolls back on failure)

Without options: the version installed on disk, the version running, a new version found, the auto-update switch, and how the last update went.
Switching versions needs a restart, and a restart interrupts a running turn (never replayed), so by default it waits until fully idle.
Before switching, it backs up the database (backups/ in the data directory) and keeps the current version's package to fall back on (update/packages/); if the new version isn't running normally within 120 seconds, it rolls back by itself.
The commands are the same on Linux, macOS and Windows, and work while Daisy is not running too (the next start backs up the database first, then tries the new version).

Options:
  --check            check the update source once now, without installing (there is no default source: --source first)
  --apply            once idle, switch to the newest version in the source (even with auto-update off); after a manual npm install -g of a new version, switch to that once idle
  --from <tgz>       with --apply: switch to this package on this machine
  --allow-downgrade  with --apply: allow switching to an older version
  --rollback         switch back to the previous version (the package kept in the data directory)
  --source <source>  set the update source (needs the PIN): a directory of .tgz files or one .tgz (absolute path), npm:@daisy-ai/daisy@latest (once this scope is registered and the package published), off; none removes it
  --now              restart right away: first lists the sessions it would interrupt, goes ahead once you confirm
  --cancel           withdraw a restart / update request not yet carried out

The restart calls can also be used directly: daisy restart status|request|cancel.

Common options: --data-dir <dir> (default: the system's convention, or DAISY_DATA); --lang <language> (or DAISY_LANG)
```

### daisy doctor

```text
Usage: daisy doctor [--json]

Self-check: Node version, data directory permissions, whether each harness is installed and signed in, PIN, ports, autostart

A read-only check: it changes nothing, and never reads or prints any credential (harness sign-in status is checked with their own read-only commands).
The exit code is 1 when anything shows ✗.

Common options: --data-dir <dir> (default: the system's convention, or DAISY_DATA); --lang <language> (or DAISY_LANG)
```

### daisy uninstall

```text
Usage: daisy uninstall [--yes]

Clean up before uninstalling: stop Daisy and remove autostart; the data directory is kept

In order: stop Daisy (a running turn is marked interrupted) → end the harness processes it left → disable and remove autostart → check that no background process or autostart entry is left.
The data directory (sessions, settings, keys, backups from before updates) is not deleted; at the end you are told where it is and how to delete it. The command itself is uninstalled last with the package manager (the same on Linux, macOS and Windows):
  npm uninstall -g --prefix <the npm global directory of this install> @daisy-ai/daisy (daisy uninstall prints the exact command for this install at the end)

Options:
  --yes    don't ask for confirmation (for scripts)

Common options: --data-dir <dir> (default: the system's convention, or DAISY_DATA); --lang <language> (or DAISY_LANG)
```

### daisy autostart

```text
Usage: daisy autostart [on | off]

Turn start-at-login on or off (Linux: a systemd user unit; macOS: a launchd login item; Windows: the current user's Run entry; never needs root / administrator)

on: on Linux, creates and enables a systemd user unit (~/.config/systemd/user/daisy.service); on macOS, writes a LaunchAgent (~/Library/LaunchAgents/ai.daisy.daisy.plist) that launchd starts after you log in; on Windows, writes a Run entry for the current user (Daisy under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) that Daisy's Windows supervisor starts after you sign in. After that, daisy start / stop go through systemd / launchd / that supervisor.
off: disables and removes it (a running Daisy is not affected; it no longer starts at the next boot / login).
Without an argument: shows the current state.
On macOS, keep it on: launchd starts it in your login session, the only way Claude's keychain sign-in can be read.

Common options: --data-dir <dir> (default: the system's convention, or DAISY_DATA); --lang <language> (or DAISY_LANG)
```

### daisy watch

```text
Usage: daisy watch [--after <seq>] [--cursor-file <file>] [--wait <seconds>] [--max <count>]

Follow the event outlet: AI approval requests, AI questions and calls waiting for approval, as they appear and are settled

One event per line on standard output (CloudEvents 1.0 JSON, see docs/contracts/events.md); status notes go to standard error.
Without --after and without a cursor file, it first takes a snapshot (every card not yet settled), then reads on from the snapshot's sequence number; after that it long-polls and prints new events as they arrive.
When Daisy restarts or can't be reached for a while, it waits for it and reads on from the same sequence number; when that number can't be continued (old events cleared, data rebuilt), it takes a new snapshot.

Options:
  --after <seq>          start reading after this sequence number (no snapshot)
  --cursor-file <file>   keep the sequence number read in this file (saved after each page) and read on from it next time; stopping mid-page reads the same page again, so de-duplicate by the event's id
  --wait <seconds>       the longest each wait lasts (1–30, default 30)
  --max <count>          exit after printing this many events (for scripts)

Just one page: daisy events list --after <seq>; a snapshot: daisy events snapshot.

Common options: --data-dir <dir> (default: the system's convention, or DAISY_DATA); --lang <language> (or DAISY_LANG)
```

## API commands

### daisy access

```text
Usage: daisy access <subcommand> …

Subcommands:
  external off      Turn off the outside face
  external on       Turn on or change the outside face (listen address, port, TLS, switches such as the terminal) (needs the PIN)
  issuer refresh    Fetch the external issuer's key set again now
  issuer remove     Stop trusting the external issuer and go back to self-issuing
  issuer set        Configure an external issuer (trust the tokens it signs) (needs the PIN)
  issuer show       Show the token issuer: self-issued or external issuer, who the owner is, the cached public keys
  passcode          Set the local web page's passcode: auto (default), on, off (needs the PIN)
  show              Show the two faces and the passcode: where they listen, where the port comes from, whether the passcode is on
  ui-origins clear  Clear the allowed external UI origins
  ui-origins set    Set the allowed external UI origins (replaces the whole list) (needs the PIN)
  ui-origins show   Show the allowed external UI origins (external UIs in a browser, CORS)

Each subcommand's arguments: daisy access <subcommand> --help
```

#### daisy access external off

```text
Usage: daisy access external off

Turn off the outside face

Narrows who can connect, so no PIN needed. Web sessions on the outside face are voided along with it.

API: DELETE /api/access/external (settings.externalOff)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy access external on

```text
Usage: daisy access external on [options]

Turn on or change the outside face (listen address, port, TLS, switches such as the terminal)

Widens who can connect, so it needs the PIN. Turning it on enables the passcode automatically. Plain HTTP is allowed only on loopback, overlay network or private network addresses (127/8, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 100.64/10, ::1, fc00::/7). TLS uses the self-signed certificate in keys/: a new one is generated only when there is none yet, when it does not cover the listen address, or when it expires within a day (written to the log and the audit); when the certificate files exist but cannot be used (wrong owner, key and certificate not a pair, unreadable), it answers 409 `tls_refused` and does not quietly replace the certificate.

Options:
  --host                   Listen address: overlay network address, 0.0.0.0, loopback address (for other programs on the same machine to visit), etc.; do not write localhost (string, 1–253 characters, required)
  --port                   Port; if empty, derived from the uid (from 29600) (integer, 1024–65535)
  --tls                    TLS by default (self-signed certificate); false (plain HTTP) is allowed only on loopback, overlay network or private network addresses (boolean, default true)
  --allow                  Open the terminal, command execution and directory browsing on the outside face (all off by default) (object, default {"terminal":false,"shell":false,"browse":false})

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: PUT /api/access/external (settings.externalOn)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy access issuer refresh

```text
Usage: daisy access issuer refresh

Fetch the external issuer's key set again now

Normally fetched automatically according to the cache headers (every hour if there are none), and also on an unknown kid; use this after the issuer rotates its keys if you want that to take effect immediately.

API: POST /api/access/issuer/refresh (settings.issuerRefresh)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy access issuer remove

```text
Usage: daisy access issuer remove

Stop trusting the external issuer and go back to self-issuing

Narrows who can connect, no PIN needed (like turning off the outside face). The cached public keys and the owner's token are deleted too, and tokens obtained for the AI are no longer renewed.

API: DELETE /api/access/issuer (settings.issuerRemove)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy access issuer set

```text
Usage: daisy access issuer set [options]

Configure an external issuer (trust the tokens it signs)

A kind of "letting someone in": from then on, tokens the issuer signs for the owner get the owner's identity (no pairing needed), and tokens signed for anyone else can only use the A2A entry. Needs the PIN, and the AI cannot do it. When configuring, the metadata and key set are fetched once, and nothing is saved if they cannot be fetched; after that, verification is offline, with key rotation by kid.

Options:
  --issuer                 The issuer identifier; must equal the iss of the tokens it signs: an https address (http only on this machine's loopback 127.0.0.1 / [::1], with DAISY_ALLOW_HTTP_ISSUER=1 set and no other people's accounts on this machine — for tests and local deployments) (string, 8–2048 characters, required)
  --metadata-url           Metadata address (RFC 8414 / OpenID Connect Discovery); derived from the issuer identifier when left out: an https address (http only on this machine's loopback 127.0.0.1 / [::1], with DAISY_ALLOW_HTTP_ISSUER=1 set and no other people's accounts on this machine — for tests and local deployments) (string, 8–2048 characters)
  --jwks-uri               Public key set (JWKS) address; taken from the metadata when left out: an https address (http only on this machine's loopback 127.0.0.1 / [::1], with DAISY_ALLOW_HTTP_ISSUER=1 set and no other people's accounts on this machine — for tests and local deployments) (string, 8–2048 characters)
  --token-endpoint         Token endpoint (RFC 8693 token exchange); taken from the metadata when left out: an https address (http only on this machine's loopback 127.0.0.1 / [::1], with DAISY_ALLOW_HTTP_ISSUER=1 set and no other people's accounts on this machine — for tests and local deployments) (string, 8–2048 characters)
  --owner-subject          Which subject (sub) is this Daisy's owner: only its tokens get the owner's identity (string, 1–256 characters, required)
  --audience               This Daisy's audience identifier at the issuer, used to verify the token's aud; if empty, this Daisy's URN (string, 1–512 characters)
  --client-id              The client id used when proving itself to the token endpoint (private_key_jwt); if empty, this Daisy's URN plus #client (string, 1–512 characters)
  --owner-token            The owner's token (signed by the issuer for the owner, without act, lifetime exp - iat at most 24 hours): used only to exchange tokens for the AI (subject_token), not to log in to this Daisy; stored in a file only the owner can read (read from standard input or a prompt, never from the command line, 16–8192 characters)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: PUT /api/access/issuer (settings.issuerSet)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy access issuer show

```text
Usage: daisy access issuer show

Show the token issuer: self-issued or external issuer, who the owner is, the cached public keys

The answer includes this Daisy's public key (JWK): register it with the external issuer so the issuer can verify the client assertion (private_key_jwt) when Daisy exchanges tokens for the AI. Contains no tokens.

API: GET /api/access/issuer (settings.issuerShow)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

```text
Usage: daisy access show

Show the two faces and the passcode: where they listen, where the port comes from, whether the passcode is on
```

```text
Usage: daisy access ui-origins clear

Clear the allowed external UI origins

Narrows who can connect, no PIN needed (like turning off the outside face). Realtime channels already connected are disconnected at the next change.

API: DELETE /api/access/ui-origins (settings.uiOriginsClear)

  -h, --help               show this help
```

#### daisy access ui-origins set

```text
Usage: daisy access ui-origins set [options]

Set the allowed external UI origins (replaces the whole list)

A kind of "letting someone in": the listed web pages can carry a token the external issuer signed for the owner and, in the browser, call the local API and the realtime channel as the owner through the outside face (the local face does not accept them), so it needs the PIN and the AI cannot do it. Requests from these origins accept only tokens the external issuer gave the owner; web sessions and local credentials are always refused.

Options:
  --origins                Allowed external UI origins, each written as `https://host[:port]` (no path, no trailing slash, no wildcards); `http://` is allowed only for local loopback (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1], for development). Empty list = none allowed (string[], ≤ 16 items, required)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: PUT /api/access/ui-origins (settings.uiOriginsSet)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy access ui-origins show

```text
Usage: daisy access ui-origins show

Show the allowed external UI origins (external UIs in a browser, CORS)

External UIs running in a browser (such as an organisation platform's web page) call the local API from these origins through the outside face (it applies only on the outside face; the local face accepts no other origin). A UI backend inside a server process sends no Origin and does not need this setting.

API: GET /api/access/ui-origins (settings.uiOriginsShow)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

### daisy agent

```text
Usage: daisy agent <subcommand> …

Subcommands:
  act set          Set whether an agent allows "act" and which permission mode act uses (needs the PIN)
  act show         Show how an agent accepts "ask" and "act": whether act is allowed, act's permission mode, ask's read-only strength (needs the PIN)
  audience set     Change an agent's audience and named-people list (needs the PIN)
  audience show    Show an agent's audience (everyone mutually recognised, or only named people) (needs the PIN)
  list             List the agents others can call (public agents and resident agents) and each one's audience (needs the PIN)
  public set       Make a session a public agent, or make it private again (needs the PIN)
  public show      See whether a session is a public agent and whether it can be made public now
  resident close   Close a resident agent: it stops accepting calls, tasks in progress stop, dedicated sessions close (records are kept)
  resident create  Create a resident agent (needs the PIN)
  resident delete  Delete a resident agent and all its dedicated sessions
  resident list    List resident agents (needs the PIN)
  resident pause   Pause a resident agent: later calls are refused (AGENT_PAUSED)
  resident resume  Resume a paused resident agent (needs the PIN)
  resident set     Change a resident agent: name, prompt, permission mode, directories, tools, concurrency, usage, how confirmations are handled (needs the PIN)
  resident show    Show a resident agent: configuration, layered prompts, usage, visiting conversations (needs the PIN)

Each subcommand's arguments: daisy agent <subcommand> --help
```

#### daisy agent act set

```text
Usage: daisy agent act set <aid> [options]

Set whether an agent allows "act" and which permission mode act uses

A kind of "letting someone in" (kind agent-exposure): needs the PIN, and the AI cannot do it. Allowing act means letting others work on the main line under this permission mode; once it is turned off, acts still queued and not yet started are withdrawn (rejected with ACT_DISABLED), and those running finish as usual. The permission mode cannot be one that skips all confirmations. A public agent without a read-only mode (unable to accept ask) cannot turn act off (409 `act_required`: make it private first).

Arguments:
  <aid>                    The agent's id (string, 1–200 characters, required)

Options:
  --act                    Whether act is allowed: true lets others, with an "act" mark, ask this AI to work on the main line (queued after your current turn); false turns it off, so calls with the mark are all rejected (ACT_DISABLED), while ask stays available (boolean)
  --permission-mode        Which permission mode act uses: one of this AI's permission modes (the modes from GET), or session = follow the session's own (the profile's). Cannot be a mode that skips all confirmations (string, 1–40 characters)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: PUT /api/agents/:aid/act (grant.actSet)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy agent act show

```text
Usage: daisy agent act show <aid>

Show how an agent accepts "ask" and "act": whether act is allowed, act's permission mode, ask's read-only strength

Ask's read-only strength and where it runs come from this AI's capability declaration: strong / weak (relying only on the harness's plan mode) / none (cannot ask, act only); branch (read-only side branch) / main-queue (no side questions or forking, so it falls back to queueing on the main line, still read-only). Read-only: owner entries such as the web page need no PIN; the local command line does.

Arguments:
  <aid>                    The agent's id (for a public agent, its session id) (string, 1–200 characters, required)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: GET /api/agents/:aid/act (grant.actShow)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy agent audience set

```text
Usage: daisy agent audience set <aid> [options]

Change an agent's audience and named-people list

One of two: open to everyone mutually recognised, or open only to named people. Needs the PIN. Narrowing takes effect immediately: calls in progress from people no longer in the audience are stopped, and waiting cards are voided. Whether it can be called at all (public, resident, private) is not changed here.

Arguments:
  <aid>                    The agent's id (string, 1–200 characters, required)

Options:
```

```text
Usage: daisy agent list

List the agents others can call (public agents and resident agents) and each one's audience

Three kinds of agent: private agents are all other sessions and are not listed here; a public agent is a session set to public (`daisy agent public set`); a resident agent is a configuration (`daisy agent resident …`). Each comes with its audience, whether act is allowed, and its number of cards waiting for approval and of always-allow grants. Read-only: the web page, paired devices and tokens an external issuer gave the owner need no PIN, the local command line does (a command-line credential may be the owner's AI); `daisy:grant` is still required, so the AI and visitors cannot read it.

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: GET /api/agents (grant.agentList)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy agent public set

```text
Usage: daisy agent public set <id> <public>

Make a session a public agent, or make it private again

A kind of "letting someone in" (kind agent-exposure): needs the PIN, and the AI cannot do it. **A public agent mixes conversations**: when visitors ask it, they can read the main line's context, and answers may reveal the owner's own work; requests marked "act" go into the main line, and the question and answer stay in the main line. For an outward service where conversations stay apart, use a resident agent. Once it is public, who can call it is decided by the audience (by default open to everyone mutually recognised, with a card on the first call; `PUT /api/agents/:aid/audience`). Refusals (409): the session is archived (`session_archived`); it is an "ask-only" side branch or a resident agent's session (`not_publishable`); the session's identity skips all confirmations (`bypass_not_private`); this AI has no read-only mode and cannot accept "ask", while "act" is off (`act_required`: such an agent can be public only when act is allowed). Making it private again takes effect immediately: outside tasks in progress or queued are stopped (rejected), cards waiting for approval are voided, and its grants, audience and ask/act settings are cleared as well; side effects already produced are not rolled back. If it is already in that state, nothing changes.

Arguments:
  <id>                     The session's id (a public agent's id is the same) (string, 1–200 characters, required)
  <public>                 true: make it public (people you mutually recognise can call it over A2A according to the audience; conversations mix, see the description); false: make it private again (calls in progress stop; grants, audience and ask/act settings are cleared) (boolean, required)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: PUT /api/sessions/:id/public (grant.publicSet)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy agent resident close

```text
Usage: daisy agent resident close <aid>

Close a resident agent: it stops accepting calls, tasks in progress stop, dedicated sessions close (records are kept)

No PIN needed: closing only takes back and lets nobody in. Its grants, audience and cards waiting for approval are deleted with it, calls in progress stop (refused), and its card and address go away; the dedicated sessions are archived and their processes stopped, with records kept and readable. A closed agent cannot be resumed; to offer the service again, create a new one.

Arguments:
  <aid>                    Resident agent id (string, 1–200 characters, required)

API: POST /api/residents/:aid/close (grant.residentClose)

Common options:

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy agent resident create

```text
Usage: daisy agent resident create [options]

Create a resident agent

A kind of "let someone in" (kind agent-exposure): needs the PIN, and the AI cannot do it. Once created, it can be called by mutually recognised people (the audience defaults to everyone mutually recognised, and the first call raises a card; narrow it with `daisy agent audience set`). Each visiting conversation starts its own dedicated session, and they cannot see one another. The profile cannot be in a mode that skips all confirmations.

Options:
  --name                   Name: the title on the agent's card (string, 1–64 characters, required)
  --description            One sentence on what service it offers (the card's description) (string, ≤ 500 characters)
  --role                   Prompt layer two, "role": who it is and what service it offers to others (string, ≤ 20000 characters)
  --instructions           Prompt layer three, "instructions": how to answer, what it may and may not do (string, ≤ 20000 characters)
  --knowledge              Prompt layer four, "knowledge": background material it can cite (string, ≤ 20000 characters)
  --permission-mode        Permission mode: one of this harness's permission modes, or session = follow the profile's. Defaults to auto (when the harness has it). Cannot be a mode that skips all confirmations (string, 1–40 characters)
  --dirs                   Directories it may use besides the workspace (absolute paths, repeatable); only harnesses that declare support can set this (Claude Code) (string[], ≤ 20 items)
  --tools                  Built-in harness tools it may use (repeatable, e.g. Read, Grep, Glob); * means the harness's full default set. Only harnesses that declare support can set this (Claude Code) (string[], ≤ 64 items)
  --concurrency            Maximum visiting conversations at once (default 4); tasks beyond that wait queued as "submitted" and are not dropped (integer, 1–32)
  --daily-turns            Maximum turns per 24 hours (0 = unlimited, at most 1000); calls past the limit are refused with QUOTA_EXCEEDED (integer, 0–1000)
  --approvals              Operations that still need a person's confirmation in auto mode: reject = refuse automatically (default; the task continues or fails without waiting); owner = send to the owner to confirm (the task stays working) ("reject" | "owner")
  --harness                Which harness to use (claude, codex, kimi, opencode, ...) (string, 1–64 characters, required)
  --workspace-id           Workspace id (listed by `daisy workspace catalog`) (string, 1–200 characters, required)
  --profile-id             Profile id (listed by `daisy workspace catalog`): must be for this harness and on the device where the workspace lives (string, 1–200 characters, required)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: POST /api/residents (grant.residentCreate)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy audit list

```text
Usage: daisy audit list [options]

View the audit: who, through which entry, did what to what, the result, the trace id

Paged from newest to oldest. Every local API action (except reads), every refusal, every tool the AI uses, and each handler's own domain records (such as pin.*, session.create) are here; records caused by the same action share a trace id. Only the owner can view it (web page, paired devices, command line); the AI's work credential cannot. Reading the audit is itself recorded too.

Options:
  --limit                  Maximum number of records (1–500, default 100), newest to oldest (integer, 1–500, default 100)
  --before                 Paging: the next from the previous page's answer (string)
  --since                  Only those at or after this time (milliseconds) (integer, ≥ 0)
  --until                  Only those before this time (milliseconds) (integer, ≥ 0)
  --channel                Only this channel's: web, device, cli, issuer, a2a, ai, system, none ("web" | "device" | "cli" | "issuer" | "a2a" | "ai" | "system" | "none")
  --route                  Only this endpoint's (e.g. session.cancel) or tool's (e.g. tool.wakeup) (string, 1–100 characters)
  --action                 Only this action's (e.g. api.session.create, access.denied, pin.grant) (string, 1–100 characters)
  --actor                  Only this kind of identity's ("owner" | "cli" | "ai" | "visitor" | "anonymous" | "system")
  --outcome                Only this outcome's: ok, denied, error ("ok" | "denied" | "error")
  --session                Only this session's AI (or what was done for its turn) (string, 1–200 characters)
  --trace                  Only this trace id's (string)

API: GET /api/audit (system.auditList)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy contact export

```text
Usage: daisy contact export [options]

Export your identity card (a piece of text you can copy)

The card holds a display name, this Daisy's public key and identity number, and addresses where it can be reached, signed by the identity key. Send the text to the other person (or save it as a .daisycard file); once they import it, they recognise you (mutual recognition needs each side to import once). The card itself carries no permissions. Read-only: owner entries such as the web page need no PIN; the local command line does.

Options:
  --name                   Display name on the card; if omitted, the owner's account name on this machine (string, 1–64 characters)
  --note                   A one-line note, e.g. "the server at work" (string, ≤ 200 characters)
  --direct                 Direct addresses (this Daisy's outside face root address); can be several. If neither this nor relay is given, the address the outside face is listening on is used (no address if it is off) (string[], ≤ 8 items)
  --relay                  Fixed addresses given by the relay; can be several (string[], ≤ 8 items)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: GET /api/contacts/me (grant.contactExport)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy contact import

```text
Usage: daisy contact import [card] [options]

Import someone's identity card (add it to contacts), optionally adding them to the allowlist too

A kind of "letting someone in": needs the PIN, and the AI cannot do it. The card is verified first (signature, identity number, human-readable lines); you cannot add yourself; a person already in contacts is replaced only with update, and an older card cannot replace a newer one. Only once added are the tokens they sign recognised; mutual recognition by itself carries no call permission, and only ticking the allowlist pre-approves them.

Arguments:
  <card>                   The card's text: the whole block the other person exported (a few human-readable lines plus a final line daisy-card:1:…), or just that last line; line breaks and spaces inserted in the middle are removed (string, 1–16384 characters)

Options:
  --card-file <file>       Card file (.daisycard, same content as the text); use either this or card (a file path; the file's content is sent, ≤ 32768 characters)
  --whitelist              Also add them to the allowlist: when they call your agents that are "open to everyone mutually recognised", no card pops up. When updating an existing contact, leaving it out keeps it as it is (boolean)
  --update                 When this person is already in contacts, replace the old card with this (newer) one; if omitted, answers 409 and lists the differences (boolean)
  --expect-id              The identity number you checked with the other person (the first 16 or more characters are enough): the card is refused if its identity number does not match (string, ≤ 200 characters)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: POST /api/contacts (grant.contactImport)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

```text
Reads only the text you give it; does not read or change contacts. Read-only: owner entries such as the web page need no PIN; the local command line does; it still needs `daisy:grant`, and the AI cannot call it.

Arguments:
  <card>                   The card's text: the whole block the other person exported (a few human-readable lines plus a final line daisy-card:1:…), or just that last line; line breaks and spaces inserted in the middle are removed (string, 1–16384 characters)

Options:
  --card-file <file>       Card file (.daisycard, same content as the text); use either this or card (a file path; the file's content is sent, ≤ 32768 characters)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: POST /api/contacts/inspect (grant.contactInspect)
```

### daisy events

```text
Usage: daisy events <subcommand> …

Subcommands:
  list      Read the event outlet incrementally by sequence number (long polling supported)
  snapshot  Snapshot of the event outlet: all cards not yet settled, and the sequence number to continue from

Each subcommand's arguments: daisy events <subcommand> --help
```

#### daisy events list

```text
Usage: daisy events list [options]

Read the event outlet incrementally by sequence number (long polling supported)

Each event is a CloudEvents 1.0 event (docs/contracts/events.md): an AI asking for approval, an AI asking a question, someone's call waiting for approval — each with an "opened" and a "resolved" kind. Ordered by `seq`, ascending; `cursor` is the last event's `seq` on this page (equal to `after` when the page is empty), to pass as `after` next time; when `hasMore` is true, read on at once.

With no new event within `wait` seconds (at most 30) the answer is an empty page; a new event is answered at once.

Resuming after a disconnect: a subscriber saves `cursor` after it has handled a page and reads on from it after a restart; it may read the same batch again — deduplicate by `id`. An `after` older than the events still kept (already cleaned up), or larger than the highest sequence number this Daisy has written (its data was rebuilt), answers 410 with `code: cursor_reset`: take a snapshot first, then read on from the snapshot's `cursor`.

With nobody subscribed nothing happens: events are written all the same and cleaned up after 30 days; an "opened" event of a card not yet resolved is kept until it is resolved.

Options:
  --after                  Answer only events whose seq is greater than this (the cursor from the last answer), default 0 (integer, ≥ 0)
  --limit                  How many at most; default 200 (integer, 1–200)
  --wait                   Long poll: with no new events, wait at most this many seconds (0–30); a new event is answered at once (integer, 0–30)

API: GET /api/events (events.list)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy events snapshot

```text
Usage: daisy events snapshot

Snapshot of the event outlet: all cards not yet settled, and the sequence number to continue from

Answers the "appeared" event of every card not yet settled (in ascending `seq`), plus `cursor`: use it afterwards as `after` for `GET /api/events` and no event after the snapshot will be missed. Use it on first subscribing or on receiving `cursor_reset`.

API: GET /api/events/snapshot (events.snapshot)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

```text
  6. daisy login show <flow id>                    done when status becomes complete; cancel with daisy login cancel <flow id>
Claude with an API key: daisy profile create --agent claude --auth-mode apiKey --node-id <node id> --label "My key" --api-key (prompts for the key, not echoed).
```

### daisy pair

```text
Usage: daisy pair [options]

Make a pairing code (daisy pair): another device that enters it connects as the owner

A kind of "letting someone in" (kind device): needs the PIN; the AI cannot do it. A pairing code is valid for 10 minutes, works once, and only on the outside face (first turn on the outside face's listener or choose a relay, both with the PIN). The answer holds the code itself and a link (the code is after #, so it never reaches the request line or the logs; the web page draws it as a QR code). With the outside face's listener on, the link is direct (a relay operator could get a certificate for the relay's address), and the relay's link is given separately (`relayUrl`, `relayWarning`); with only a relay, the relay's link is given and `warning` says plainly that the relay operator can obtain the pairing code and the device credential; when the relay has only a self-signed certificate no link is given (`url: null`), just the code to type in on the device, with a warning not to click through certificate warnings. At most 5 unused codes at once; making another pushes out the oldest. 5 wrong codes from one source (the direct listener's address; through a relay, the address the relay reports) pause that source for 15 minutes (other sources go on); 20 wrong codes from all sources together void the codes of that period. `wasLocked` and `recentFailures` in the answer say someone typed a wrong code. Resetting or changing the PIN voids the unused codes and lifts the pauses too.

Options:
  --name                   A name for this device; if empty, the name the device reports itself (the browser name) is used (string, 1–60 characters)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: POST /api/devices/pair (settings.pair)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy pin reset

```text
Usage: daisy pin reset [options]

Reset the PIN locally (clears the PIN and all PIN grants)

Only done on the local command line (local credential); the web page, paired devices and the AI cannot call it. A reset clears the PIN and all PIN grants, withdraws trust in the external issuer and the stored owner tokens, turns off the outside face and voids its web sessions and one-time passcodes, revokes all outside grants, mutually recognised cards and paired devices, and records an audit entry; afterwards the PIN can only be set again on the local command line.

Options:
  --confirm                Confirm the reset: it withdraws trust in the external issuer and the stored owner tokens, and revokes all outside grants, mutually recognised cards and paired devices (true, required)

API: POST /api/pin/reset (settings.pinReset)

```

#### daisy pin set

```text
Usage: daisy pin set [options]

Set or change the PIN

The first set needs no old PIN; after a local reset it can only be set again on this machine's command line. Once a PIN is set, changing it needs the old PIN, and a wrong old PIN counts toward consecutive wrong tries just like getting a grant. After a change, all previously issued PIN grants stop working. Daisy stores only a verifier of the PIN. Until the PIN is set, Daisy starts no AI turns.

Options:
  --pin                    The new PIN (6–128 characters; digits only is fine) (read from standard input or a prompt, never from the command line, 1–512 characters, required)
  --old-pin                The old PIN: required when one is already set (read from standard input or a prompt, never from the command line, 1–512 characters)

API: POST /api/pin (settings.pinSet)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

### daisy prompt

```text
Usage: daisy prompt <subcommand> …

Subcommands:
  layers apply         "Apply now": estimate first, then confirm with the estimate's token
  layers apply-cancel  Cancel the queued items in this batch that have not started
  layers forget-node   Forget the organization core a runner reported
  layers set           Change layered prompt settings
  layers show          Show layered prompt settings, what each runner reports, and the apply queue
  mine set             Change your own prompt supplement (note and optional sections)
  mine show            Show your own prompt supplement

Each subcommand's arguments: daisy prompt <subcommand> --help
```

#### daisy prompt layers apply

```text
Usage: daisy prompt layers apply [options]

"Apply now": estimate first, then confirm with the estimate's token

Without `confirm` it only answers with the estimate and a one-time `token`; only with `confirm: true` and that `token` does it run: it compacts up to `limit` of the most recently used sessions that are not yet using the new text.

Options:
  --confirm                Confirm and run (otherwise only estimate) (boolean, default false)
  --limit                  Maximum number of sessions to compact in this batch (integer, 1–100, default 20)
  --token                  The token received with the estimate (string, ≤ 100 characters)

API: POST /api/admin/prompt-layers/apply-now (settings.layersApplyNow)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

### daisy relay

```text
Usage: daisy relay <subcommand> …

Subcommands:
  off   Stop using the relay: disconnect and remove the address from the card (needs the PIN)
  set   Choose a relay (or switch): Daisy connects out and stays connected, getting a fixed outside address (needs the PIN)
  show  Show the relay: which one is chosen, whether it is connected, the outside address, the certificate

Each subcommand's arguments: daisy relay <subcommand> --help
```

#### daisy relay off

```text
Usage: daisy relay off

Stop using the relay: disconnect and remove the address from the card

Connections going through the relay are cut immediately, and the card no longer carries the relay address. The key and certificate are kept (choosing the same relay again keeps the same address). It only narrows who can connect in, but still needs the PIN: a command-line credential may be the owner's AI using it through Bash, and it must not be able to quietly cut off the owner's reachability from other networks.

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: DELETE /api/relay (settings.relayOff)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy relay set

```text
Usage: daisy relay set <url> [options]

Choose a relay (or switch): Daisy connects out and stays connected, getting a fixed outside address

Requests arriving through the relay only reach the outside face, so choosing a relay lets anyone who can reach the relay knock on the outside face's door: it needs the PIN. The outside face's listener does not need to be on first (relay-only works too); the outside face's passcode is turned on automatically. Certificate: by default one is requested from Let's Encrypt (TLS-ALPN-01, passed through the relay); before it arrives, or if it cannot be obtained, a self-signed certificate is used, and then only Daisy-to-Daisy traffic works through the relay (they check the TLS binding statement), while third-party clients and browsers report an untrusted certificate.

Arguments:
  <url>                    The relay's own address, e.g. relay.example or https://relay.example:8443 (domain and port only) (string, 1–300 characters, required)

Options:
  --acme                   Request a certificate for the relay address from a certificate authority (ACME TLS-ALPN-01, Let's Encrypt by default). If off, only a self-signed certificate is used: then only Daisy-to-Daisy traffic works through the relay (boolean, default true)
  --acme-directory         ACME directory URL (https), Let's Encrypt by default; can be another certificate authority that supports TLS-ALPN-01 (string, 1–300 characters)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: PUT /api/relay (settings.relaySet)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy relay show

```text
Usage: daisy relay show

Show the relay: which one is chosen, whether it is connected, the outside address, the certificate

API: GET /api/relay (settings.relayShow)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

### daisy request

```text
Usage: daisy request <subcommand> …

Subcommands:
  decide  Approve or reject a call request: always allow, allow once, reject (needs the PIN)
  list    List other people's requests to call my agents (cards waiting for approval) (needs the PIN)
  show    Show a call request (needs the PIN)

Each subcommand's arguments: daisy request <subcommand> --help
```

#### daisy request decide

```text
Usage: daisy request decide <rid> <decision> [options]

Approve or reject a call request: always allow, allow once, reject

A kind of "letting someone in": needs the PIN, and the AI cannot do it. Sending the same decision again answers the original result; one already handled with a different decision, expired or voided answers 409. If things have changed by the time of approval (the other person was removed from contacts, the agent was made private again or is no longer open to them), the card is voided and it answers 409 `request_stale`.

Arguments:
  <rid>                    The request's id (`call:…`; `call:` can be omitted) (string, 1–200 characters, required)
  <decision>               Always allow (always: records a grant, so this person is not asked again when calling this agent; all waiting calls are let through), allow once (once: lets through only the call that raised this card; other calls waiting at the same time move to a new card and are asked again), reject (reject: all waiting calls are rejected, and calls again within 10 minutes are rejected outright) ("always" | "once" | "reject", required)

Options:
  --note                   A note (recorded only on the card) (string, ≤ 2000 characters)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: POST /api/requests/:rid/decision (grant.requestDecide)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy request list

```text
Usage: daisy request list [options]

List other people's requests to call my agents (cards waiting for approval)

By default lists only those waiting for approval. The same card also appears in the approval list (`GET /api/approvals`, `kind: "call"`), but can be approved or rejected only here (needs the PIN). Reading: owner entries such as the web page need no PIN; the local command line does; it still needs `daisy:grant`: the AI and visitors cannot read it.

Options:
  --status                 Waiting for approval, handled or all ("pending" | "decided" | "all", default "pending")
  --limit                  Number of items (integer, 1–200, default 100)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: GET /api/requests (grant.requestList)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy request show

```text
Usage: daisy request show <rid>

Show a call request

Read-only: owner entries such as the web page need no PIN; the local command line does.

Arguments:
  <rid>                    The request's id (`call:…`; `call:` can be omitted) (string, 1–200 characters, required)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: GET /api/requests/:rid (grant.requestShow)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

```text
Usage: daisy restart <subcommand> …

  status   Show pending updates and restarts, and what they are waiting for

Each subcommand's arguments: daisy restart <subcommand> --help
```

#### daisy restart cancel

```text
Usage: daisy restart cancel

Withdraw a restart request that has not run yet

API: DELETE /api/update/restart (settings.updateCancel)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy restart request

```text
Usage: daisy restart request [options]

Restart Daisy (when idle, or now)

`idle` waits until no work is running, then restarts; `now` restarts immediately and interrupts turns in progress: it first answers 409, listing what would be interrupted and giving a `confirm` credential; it runs only when that credential is sent back (if new work starts in the meantime, it answers 409 again with a new list and a new credential). Interrupted work is not replayed.

Options:
  --mode                   idle: wait for idle; now: immediately ("idle" | "now", default "idle")
  --confirm                The confirm credential from the last 409: confirms interrupting the work on that list (string, 1–64000 characters)

API: POST /api/update/restart (settings.updateRestart)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy restart status

```text
Usage: daisy restart status

Show pending updates and restarts, and what they are waiting for

Lists versions already installed or built that take effect once idle, the owner's restart request, and the sessions and commands running now that would be interrupted; a Daisy installed via npm also has `package`: the source, the new version found, the auto-update switch, and the result of the last update (switched / rolled back / failed, with the reason and the pre-update backup).

API: GET /api/update (settings.updateStatus)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

### daisy session

```text
Usage: daisy session <subcommand> …

Subcommands:
  activity             What the live process has been doing recently
  background stop      Stop an item under "Background" (an agent's background task or a Daisy schedule)
  cancel               Stop the session's current turn
  create               Create a session
  delete               Delete a session
  events               Read session events incrementally by sequence number
  identity fresh       Continue without history: give up the native history that cannot be carried over
  identity switch      Switch identity: the session continues with another of your profiles
  items                Page backwards: the items before a given one
  list                 List your sessions
  offline              Take a session offline: close its live process
  operation harness    Change the configuration of the harness the session uses: config files, MCP servers, plugins, skills
  operation run        Run a native operation on a session (list models, fork, rewind, compact, etc.)
  operation status     Check a native operation's status and result
  prompt apply         Compact now and put the new prompt into effect
  prompt apply-cancel  Cancel a queued "apply now"
  prompt set           Change the session's own prompt supplement
  prompt show          Show a session's layered prompts and whether they are in effect
  queue jump           Jump the queue: start a queued message immediately
  queue list           List queued messages (steered-but-unread first, then queue-jumped ones)
  queue merge-jump     Merge and jump: combine the selected queued messages into one and jump the queue
  queue merge-steer    Merge and steer: combine the selected queued messages into one and send it into the running turn
  queue remove         Remove a queued message (withdraw it if steered in but not yet read)
  queue remove-many    Remove queued messages in bulk (selected ones, or all)
  queue resume         Resume a paused queue: send the next queued message
  recovery events      Read a recovery record's events, page by page
  recovery list        List recovery records left by interrupted turns (latest 50)
  schedule add         Set a timer (one-time wake-up or recurring cron)
  schedule cancel      Cancel a timer or background command
  schedule list        List a session's timers and background commands
  schedule update      Change a timer that is still waiting
  send                 Send a message to a session
  shell run            Run a command in the session's working directory
  shell status         Read a command's status and output
  show                 Read a session: settings, items and cursor
  steer                Steer now: send a message into the running turn
  terminal input       Type text into the terminal or resize its window
  terminal open        Open a terminal in the session's working directory
  terminal output      Read terminal output incrementally by sequence number
  terminal show        The session's most recent terminal task
  update               Change a session: title, archiving, related tasks, model and reasoning effort

Common: daisy session create … → daisy session send <id> "message" → daisy session show <id>;
archive: daisy session update <id> --archived; the AI's tool approvals and questions are answered only on the web page (daisy open).

Each subcommand's arguments: daisy session <subcommand> --help
```

#### daisy session create

```text
Usage: daisy session create [options]

Create a session

`requestId` is an idempotency key: sending the same key again answers the original session (with `duplicate: true`). New sessions are always private; making a session public is a separate `daisy:grant` endpoint that needs the PIN (`daisy agent public set`).

Options:
  --workspace-mode          ("shared" | "isolated" | "read-only" | "snapshot", default "shared")
  --title                   (string, ≤ 200 characters, default "")
  --agent                   ("claude" | "codex" | "kimi" | "opencode" | "antigravity" | "deepseek", required)
  --workspace-id            (string, required)
  --profile-id              (string, required)
  --task                    (object)

Sending the same command again never runs it twice (an idempotency key is added automatically).

API: POST /api/sessions (session.create)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  --idempotency-key <key>  the idempotency key (generated by default); resending with the same key after a disconnect never runs it twice
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

```text
  --idempotency-key <key>  the idempotency key (generated by default); resending with the same key after a disconnect never runs it twice
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy session operation run

```text
Usage: daisy session operation run <id> <name> [options]

Run a native operation on a session (list models, fork, rewind, compact, etc.)

Asynchronous: answers the operation's id; query the result with `session.operationStatus`. The result of `fork` is in the new session (the answer's `sessionId`). Refused while the session has queued or running work. `args.count` for `rewind` is how many turns to rewind (1–10000, default 1). `fork`, `compact` and `rewind` (with `files: true`, it also needs "undo files when rewinding") require the session's AI to declare that capability (the snapshot's `features`); otherwise it answers 409 `capability_unsupported`, and `fix` says what to do.

Arguments:
  <id>                      (string, required)
  <name>                   Operation name (the ones that change harness settings go through `session operation harness`; opening a terminal goes through `session terminal open`) ("catalog" | "models" | "skills" | "mcp" | "plugins" | "config.read" | "fork" | "rewind" | "compact" | "review", required)

Options:
  --args                   Arguments for the operation (Record<string, any>, default {})

Sending the same command again never runs it twice (an idempotency key is added automatically).

API: POST /api/sessions/:id/operations (session.operation)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  --idempotency-key <key>  the idempotency key (generated by default); resending with the same key after a disconnect never runs it twice
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy session send

```text
Usage: daisy session send <id> <text> [options]

Send a message to a session

With `delivery: "queue"` it goes into the queue; while a turn is running it is also queued after that turn. `requestId` is an idempotency key: sending the same key again answers the original message (with `duplicate: true`). Refused while the resident agent is paused.

Arguments:
  <id>                      (string, required)
  <text>                    (string, ≤ 100000 characters, required)

Options:
  --delivery                ("normal" | "queue", default "normal")
  --attachment-ids          (string[], ≤ 8 items, default [])
  --context                 (object)
  --terminal-ids            (string[], ≤ 8 items, default [])

Sending the same command again never runs it twice (an idempotency key is added automatically).

API: POST /api/sessions/:id/messages (session.send)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  --idempotency-key <key>  the idempotency key (generated by default); resending with the same key after a disconnect never runs it twice
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

### daisy token

```text
Usage: daisy token <subcommand> …

Subcommands:
  issue   Issue a time-limited token to a third-party A2A client (daisy token) (needs the PIN)
  list    List tokens issued to third-party A2A clients (records only, not the tokens themselves) (needs the PIN)
  revoke  Revoke a token issued to a third-party A2A client (needs the PIN)

Each subcommand's arguments: daisy token <subcommand> --help
```

#### daisy token issue

```text
Usage: daisy token issue [options]

Issue a time-limited token to a third-party A2A client (daisy token)

A kind of "let someone in" (kind visitor-token): needs the PIN, and the AI cannot do it. The issued token: `iss` and `aud` are this Daisy; `sub` is that contact (yourself for `me`); `scope` is only `daisy:invoke`; `client_id` is `token:<jti>`; there is no `act`. Whoever holds it calls through A2A as that contact and still has to pass call grants (audience, allowlist, cards); one issued for `me` also only goes through the A2A entry and cannot reach the local API. The token appears only in this one answer; Daisy stores only the issue record (jti, for whom, note, expiry), not the token itself: whoever gets it can call as that identity, so keep it like a password. It is voided when the contact is removed or the PIN is reset.

Options:
  --for                    For whom: the contact's identity number (or a unique prefix of 8+ characters); me = myself (still only a visitor, only through the A2A entry, not given owner identity) (string, 1–200 characters, required)
  --ttl                    Validity: 7d, 12h, 30m or seconds; default 7 days, at most 90 days (string, ≤ 20 characters)
  --note                   Note (who it is for, what it does, e.g. "for CI") (string, ≤ 200 characters)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: POST /api/tokens (grant.tokenIssue)

Common options:
  --json <object>          start the request body from this JSON object, then apply the options (@file, - as above)
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy token list

```text
Usage: daisy token list [options]

List tokens issued to third-party A2A clients (records only, not the tokens themselves)

By default lists only those still valid; `state=all` also lists expired and revoked ones (kept 30 days). Read-only: the web page, paired devices and tokens an external issuer gave the owner need no PIN, the local command line does (a command-line credential may be the owner's AI); `daisy:grant` is still required, so the AI and visitors cannot read it.

Options:
  --state                  active: still valid; all: also expired and revoked ones (kept 30 days) ("active" | "all", default "active")

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: GET /api/tokens (grant.tokenList)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```

#### daisy token revoke

```text
Usage: daisy token revoke <jti>

Revoke a token issued to a third-party A2A client

Takes effect immediately: requests carrying it are refused (401) from the next one on. Tasks already started are not affected (to stop them, withdraw the grant or take the agent back). Needs the PIN. Revoking an already revoked token again answers with the original record.

Arguments:
  <jti>                    Token id (the jti in `daisy token list`) (string, 1–64 characters, required)

This step asks for the PIN (prompted in the terminal).

API: DELETE /api/tokens/:jti (grant.tokenRevoke)

Common options:
  -h, --help               show this help

The answer is printed as JSON on standard output; on an error it says what happened and how to fix it, and exits non-zero.
```
